triples.source_text: Is not the Lord’s day darkness rather than light, gloom that has no brightness in it?

target_units.text: For the Lord’s great day is near, near and very swift. The sound of the Lord’s day is bitter and harsh; it is appointed mighty.
That day is a day of wrath, a day of affliction and constraint, a day of untimely ruin and destruction, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and mist,

triples.relationship: shared description of the Lord's day as gloom
triples.rationale: Amos asks whether the Lord's day is darkness and gloom without brightness. Zephaniah likewise calls the near Lord's day a day of darkness, gloom, cloud and mist within an announcement of wrath.

triples.source_text: “I have hated and rejected your festivals, and I certainly will not smell a pleasing scent in your festal gatherings,

target_units.text: you will no longer continue. If you bring fine flour, it is futile. Incense is an abomination to Me. Your new moons and sabbaths and a great day I cannot endure; fasting and idleness,
and your new moons and your festivals My soul hates. You have become more than enough for Me; I will no longer let your sins go.

triples.relationship: the Lord's rejection of religious festivals
triples.rationale: Amos's divine speaker hates and rejects the people's festivals and festal gatherings. Isaiah likewise declares that His soul hates their festivals and cannot endure their observances. Both challenge the acceptability of outward religious celebrations.

triples.source_text: because even if you bring Me whole burnt offerings and your sacrifices, I will not receive them, and I will not look upon the salvation offering of your display.

target_units.text: Hear, earth! Behold, I am bringing evils upon this people, the fruit of their turning away, because they did not attend to My words and rejected My law.
Why do you bring Me frankincense from Sheba and cinnamon from a distant land? Your whole burnt offerings are not acceptable, and your sacrifices did not please Me.

triples.relationship: burnt offerings and sacrifices declared unacceptable
triples.rationale: Amos's divine speaker refuses the people's whole burnt offerings and sacrifices. Jeremiah likewise declares burnt offerings unacceptable and sacrifices displeasing after saying that the people rejected God's words and law.

triples.source_text: Remove from Me the sound of your songs; I will not listen to the music of your instruments,

target_units.text: Whenever you stretch your hands toward Me, I will turn My eyes away from you. Even if you multiply supplication, I will not listen to you, for your hands are full of blood.

triples.rationale: Amos's divine speaker will not listen to instrumental music in the sequence of rejected festivals and offerings. Isaiah likewise says He will not listen to multiplied supplications because the people's hands are full of blood. One passage names music and the other prayer, while both reject religious expression.

triples.source_text: and judgment shall roll as water, and righteousness as an impassable torrent.

target_units.text: If you had listened to My commands, your peace would have become like a river and your righteousness like a sea wave.

triples.rationale: Amos pictures judgment rolling as water and righteousness as an impassable torrent. Isaiah likewise uses a river for peace and a sea wave for righteousness. The comparison concerns moving-water imagery, without making the passages' surrounding statements identical.

triples.source_text: Did you offer Me slaughtered offerings and sacrifices in the wilderness for forty years, house of Israel?

target_units.text: But God turned away and handed them over to worship the host of heaven, as it is written in the book of the prophets: ‘Did you offer Me slaughtered victims and sacrifices for forty years in the wilderness, house of Israel?

triples.relationship: explicit later quotation of the wilderness-sacrifice question
triples.rationale: Amos asks Israel's house whether it offered sacrifices in the wilderness for forty years. Acts explicitly introduces words from the prophets and repeats that question about sacrifices, forty years and the wilderness.

triples.source_text: You took up the tent of Moloch and the star of your god Raiphan, their figures that you made for yourselves.

target_units.text: You took up the tent of Moloch and the star of your god Raiphan, the images you made to worship them. And I will deport you beyond Babylon.’

triples.relationship: explicit later quotation about Moloch and Raiphan
triples.rationale: Amos names Moloch's tent, the star of the god Raiphan and figures made by the people. Acts' prophetic quotation repeats these named objects and the making of their images, adding that the images were made for worship.

triples.source_text: I will deport you beyond Damascus,” says the Lord; God Almighty is His name.

target_units.text: You took up the tent of Moloch and the star of your god Raiphan, the images you made to worship them. And I will deport you beyond Babylon.’

triples.relationship: later quotation with a different deportation destination
triples.rationale: Amos announces deportation beyond Damascus. Acts' quotation following the same Moloch-and-Raiphan charge announces deportation beyond Babylon. The corresponding deportation statement is retained together with the explicit difference in destination.

triples.source_text: sleeping upon ivory beds and indulging upon your couches, eating young goats from the flocks and milk-fed calves from the herds,

target_units.text: Now there was a certain rich man, and he clothed himself in purple and fine linen, enjoying himself in splendor every day.
And a certain poor man named Lazarus had been laid at his gateway, covered with sores
and longing to be filled with what fell from the rich man’s table. Even the dogs came and licked his sores.

triples.rationale: Amos pictures ivory beds, couches and choice meat in a passage that proceeds to indifference toward Joseph's shattering. Luke likewise places a rich man's daily splendor and table beside the afflicted Lazarus longing for its food. The comparison concerns luxury juxtaposed with suffering.

triples.source_text: clapping to the sound of instruments; they reckoned them as lasting, not passing away,

target_units.text: Woe to those rising in the morning and pursuing strong drink, lingering into the evening, for wine will burn them up!
For with lyre and harp, drums and flutes they drink wine, but they do not look at the Lord’s works or consider the works of His hands.

triples.rationale: Amos describes clapping to instruments within the sequence of luxurious dining and wine drinking. Isaiah likewise describes lyre, harp, drums and flutes accompanying wine while condemning lack of attention to the Lord's works. The shared scene is musical indulgence; Amos's statement about things reckoned lasting is not replaced.

triples.source_text: drinking strained wine and anointing yourselves with the finest perfumes, yet suffering nothing over Joseph’s shattering.

target_units.text: The Lord Sabaoth called on that day for weeping, lamentation, shaving and putting on sackcloth,
but they made gladness and exultation, slaughtering calves and sacrificing sheep to eat meat and drink wine, saying, “Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die!”

triples.relationship: wine and pleasure when mourning is called for
triples.rationale: Amos describes wine and fine perfumes without suffering over Joseph's shattering. Isaiah likewise contrasts a divine call to weeping and lamentation with gladness, meat and wine. Both expose pleasure pursued in the face of a need to mourn.

triples.source_text: Therefore now they will be captives from the foremost of the powerful, and horses’ neighing will be removed from Ephraim.

target_units.text: Woe to those rising in the morning and pursuing strong drink, lingering into the evening, for wine will burn them up!
For with lyre and harp, drums and flutes they drink wine, but they do not look at the Lord’s works or consider the works of His hands.
Therefore My people became captive because they did not know the Lord, and there was a multitude of dead through famine and thirst for water.

triples.rationale: Amos announces captivity after the descriptions of luxurious food, music, wine and indifference. Isaiah likewise moves from strong drink, instruments and neglect of the Lord's works to the people's captivity. Both place that outcome after the account of indulgence.

triples.source_text: For the Lord swore by Himself: “I abhor all Jacob’s arrogance and have hated his regions; I will remove the city with all who inhabit it.”

target_units.text: But if you do not carry out these words, I swear by Myself, says the Lord, that this house will become a desolation.

triples.rationale: Amos introduces the Lord swearing by Himself before announcing removal of the city and its inhabitants. Jeremiah likewise records Him swearing by Himself that the royal house will become a desolation if His commands are not carried out.

triples.source_text: If ten men remain in one house, they will die, and those left over will remain.

target_units.text: For thus says the Lord, the Lord: “From the city out of which a thousand went, a hundred will remain, and from the one out of which a hundred went, ten will remain for Israel’s house.”

triples.relationship: same-book warnings of shrinking numbers of survivors
triples.rationale: Amos 5 reduces the remaining numbers from cities, including a hundred reduced to ten. Amos 6 describes ten remaining in a house and announces their death while also mentioning those left over remaining. Both develop the book's population-loss warnings without identifying the groups as the same people.

triples.source_text: For look, the Lord commands, and He will strike the great house with fractures and the small house with cracks.

target_units.text: and I will confound and strike the colonnaded house along with the summer house. Ivory houses will perish, and many other houses will be added,” says the Lord.

triples.relationship: same-book destruction reaching different kinds of houses
triples.rationale: Amos 6 announces fractures in the great house and cracks in the small house. Chapter 3 likewise announces striking colonnaded and summer houses and the loss of ivory houses. Both portray judgment reaching different kinds of dwellings, with distinct categories in each passage.

triples.source_text: Will horses pursue upon rocks? Will they remain silent among females? For you turned judgment into anger and the fruit of righteousness into bitterness,

target_units.text: For the vineyard of the Lord Sabaoth is Israel’s house, and the man of Judah a beloved new planting. I waited for it to produce judgment, but it produced lawlessness, not righteousness but an outcry.

triples.relationship: judgment and righteousness transformed into harmful results
triples.rationale: Amos accuses the people of turning judgment into anger and righteousness's fruit into bitterness. Isaiah likewise contrasts expected judgment and righteousness with the lawlessness and outcry actually produced. Both describe the failure of expected just conduct through opposed outcomes.

triples.source_text: rejoicing over nothing, saying, “Did we not acquire horns by our own strength?”

target_units.text: Do not say in your heart: My strength and the might of my hand have gotten me this great wealth.
And you shall remember the Lord your God, for He gives you strength to gain wealth, that He may establish His covenant which the Lord sware unto your fathers, as at this day.

triples.relationship: claims of achievement by one's own strength
triples.rationale: Amos quotes people claiming to have acquired horns by their own strength. Deuteronomy warns against saying that one's own strength gained wealth and instead directs remembrance of the Lord who gives strength. Both quote people crediting their own strength, while naming different things acquired.

triples.source_text: “For look, I am raising a nation against you, house of Israel, and they will crush you so that you cannot enter Emath, as far as the Wadi of the West.”

target_units.text: Behold, I am bringing a nation upon you from far away, house of Israel, says the Lord, a nation whose language’s sound you will not understand.
All are strong,

and they will devour your harvest and your bread, and devour your sons and daughters, and devour your sheep and calves, and devour your vineyards and fig orchards and olive groves; and with a sword they will thresh your fortified cities, in which you have trusted.

triples.relationship: the Lord raises a foreign nation against Israel
triples.rationale: Amos announces the Lord raising a nation against Israel to crush it. Jeremiah likewise announces bringing a distant nation against Israel, with strong attackers consuming its produce and attacking fortified cities.
